**Valley High School (VHS)** is a public high school in Lucasville in Scioto County in southern Ohio. It is the only high school in the Valley Local School District. Their nickname is the Indians, and their colors are purple and gold.
The high school building is located on a large property adjacent to the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility. The Valley Elementary School building sits on the same property northeast of the high school building. The local Kiwanis group assisted in the setting up of playground equipment on the side of the elementary building.

Both the high school and elementary were built in 1992-1993 and were scheduled to begin holding classes after the Easter break in the spring of 1993. However, a prisoner uprising on Easter Sunday at the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility, commonly referred to as the Lucasville Prison Riot,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-60_Moments:_Lucasville_Prison_Riot-3) prevented the opening of the buildings.
The high school stadium which boasts a FieldTurf surface is immediately north of the high school building and finished construction prior to the start of the school year in 2000. The high school has tennis courts as well as five baseball/softball fields, three additional soccer fields, and two football fields used for local youth sports are also located on the property. The high school baseball and softball stadiums are located on a nearby property.
Valley High School has an average graduating class size of 94 students, and the student teacher ratio is 16:1.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-Student_Teacher_Ratio_Valley_High_School-4) The number of students in grade 10 that were at or above proficiency standards exceeded the state average in all five subjects of the Ohio Graduation Test in 2011.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-Valley_High_School_Test_Scores-5)Advance Placement courses are offered in English literature and composition, U.S. government and politics, calculus, and chemistry.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-Courses-6)

There are ten school districts and eleven high schools in Scioto County along with one parochial school as well several private and community schools.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-Ohio_County_Profiles-7) The school's athletic affiliation is with the Ohio High School Athletic Association (OHSAA) and the Southern Ohio Conference (SOC), which has seventeen member schools and is divided into two divisions (SOC I & SOC II) based on the schools' enrollment. The SOC includes teams from four different Ohio counties - Jackson County (Oak Hill High School), Lawrence County (Saint Joseph Central High School and Symmes Valley High School), Pike County (Waverly High School, Eastern High School, and Western High School), and Scioto County (Clay High School, Green High School, Glenwood High School, Sciotoville Community School, Valley High School, Northwest High School, Minford High School, Portsmouth West High School, Notre Dame High School, South Webster High School, and Wheelersburg High School).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-SOC_Constitution-8)

**Valley High School (VHS)** is a public high school in Lucasville in Scioto County in southern Ohio. It is the only high school in the Valley Local School District. Their nickname is the Indians, and their colors are purple and gold.
The high school building is located on a large property adjacent to the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility. The Valley Elementary School building sits on the same property northeast of the high school building. The local Kiwanis group assisted in the setting up of playground equipment on the side of the elementary building.
texts.1:
Both the high school and elementary were built in 1992-1993 and were scheduled to begin holding classes after the Easter break in the spring of 1993. However, a prisoner uprising on Easter Sunday at the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility, commonly referred to as the Lucasville Prison Riot,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-60_Moments:_Lucasville_Prison_Riot-3) prevented the opening of the buildings.
The high school stadium which boasts a FieldTurf surface is immediately north of the high school building and finished construction prior to the start of the school year in 2000. The high school has tennis courts as well as five baseball/softball fields, three additional soccer fields, and two football fields used for local youth sports are also located on the property. The high school baseball and softball stadiums are located on a nearby property.
Valley High School has an average graduating class size of 94 students, and the student teacher ratio is 16:1.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-Student_Teacher_Ratio_Valley_High_School-4) The number of students in grade 10 that were at or above proficiency standards exceeded the state average in all five subjects of the Ohio Graduation Test in 2011.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-Valley_High_School_Test_Scores-5)Advance Placement courses are offered in English literature and composition, U.S. government and politics, calculus, and chemistry.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-Courses-6)
texts.2:
There are ten school districts and eleven high schools in Scioto County along with one parochial school as well several private and community schools.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-Ohio_County_Profiles-7) The school's athletic affiliation is with the Ohio High School Athletic Association (OHSAA) and the Southern Ohio Conference (SOC), which has seventeen member schools and is divided into two divisions (SOC I & SOC II) based on the schools' enrollment. The SOC includes teams from four different Ohio counties - Jackson County (Oak Hill High School), Lawrence County (Saint Joseph Central High School and Symmes Valley High School), Pike County (Waverly High School, Eastern High School, and Western High School), and Scioto County (Clay High School, Green High School, Glenwood High School, Sciotoville Community School, Valley High School, Northwest High School, Minford High School, Portsmouth West High School, Notre Dame High School, South Webster High School, and Wheelersburg High School).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-SOC_Constitution-8)

**Valley High School (VHS)** is a public high school in Lucasville in Scioto County in southern Ohio. It is the only high school in the Valley Local School District. Their nickname is the Indians, and their colors are purple and gold.
The high school building is located on a large property adjacent to the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility. The Valley Elementary School building sits on the same property northeast of the high school building. The local Kiwanis group assisted in the setting up of playground equipment on the side of the elementary building.

Both the high school and elementary were built in 1992-1993 and were scheduled to begin holding classes after the Easter break in the spring of 1993. However, a prisoner uprising on Easter Sunday at the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility, commonly referred to as the Lucasville Prison Riot,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-60_Moments:_Lucasville_Prison_Riot-3) prevented the opening of the buildings.
The high school stadium which boasts a FieldTurf surface is immediately north of the high school building and finished construction prior to the start of the school year in 2000. The high school has tennis courts as well as five baseball/softball fields, three additional soccer fields, and two football fields used for local youth sports are also located on the property. The high school baseball and softball stadiums are located on a nearby property.
Valley High School has an average graduating class size of 94 students, and the student teacher ratio is 16:1.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-Student_Teacher_Ratio_Valley_High_School-4) The number of students in grade 10 that were at or above proficiency standards exceeded the state average in all five subjects of the Ohio Graduation Test in 2011.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-Valley_High_School_Test_Scores-5)Advance Placement courses are offered in English literature and composition, U.S. government and politics, calculus, and chemistry.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-Courses-6)

There are ten school districts and eleven high schools in Scioto County along with one parochial school as well several private and community schools.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-Ohio_County_Profiles-7) The school's athletic affiliation is with the Ohio High School Athletic Association (OHSAA) and the Southern Ohio Conference (SOC), which has seventeen member schools and is divided into two divisions (SOC I & SOC II) based on the schools' enrollment. The SOC includes teams from four different Ohio counties - Jackson County (Oak Hill High School), Lawrence County (Saint Joseph Central High School and Symmes Valley High School), Pike County (Waverly High School, Eastern High School, and Western High School), and Scioto County (Clay High School, Green High School, Glenwood High School, Sciotoville Community School, Valley High School, Northwest High School, Minford High School, Portsmouth West High School, Notre Dame High School, South Webster High School, and Wheelersburg High School).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_High_School_(Ohio)#cite_note-SOC_Constitution-8)

**Outagamie County** ( _OW-tə-GAY-mee_)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-1) is a county in the Fox Cities region of the U.S. state of Wisconsin, in the northeast of the state. As of the 2020 census, the population was 190,705.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-2020-census-55087-2) Its county seat is Appleton.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR6-3)

Outagamie County is part of the Appleton Metropolitan Statistical Area, which is itself part of the Appleton-Neenah-OshkoshCombined Statistical Area. It was named for the historic Meskwaki (Fox) people.
"Outagamie", a French transliteration of the Anishinaabe term for the Meskwaki (Fox) people, means "dwellers of the other shore" or "dwellers on the other side of the stream",[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-4) referring to their historic habitation along the St. Lawrence River and south of the Great Lakes. They occupied considerable territory in Wisconsin before colonization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-5) Outagamie County was created in 1851 and organized in 1852.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-6) Before that, it was under the jurisdiction of Brown County.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has an area of 645 square miles (1,670 km 2), of which 638 square miles (1,650 km 2) is land and 7.1 square miles (18 km 2) (1.1%) is water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR1-7)

Outagamie County's government consists of an elected County Board of Supervisors, a County Executive, and 36 county agencies and departments.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-outagamie.org-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-9)
The county executive serves as its chief executive officer, participating in the legislative process with the County Board of Supervisors and exercising administrative authority and control over the county's operations, departments, offices, boards, programs, and communications.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-10)
Department heads are appointed by the county executive, subject to the approval of the board of supervisors. The county executive also appoints members to the county's boards and commissions. The county executive sets the annual budget in consultation with and subject to the approval of the board of supervisors.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-11)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-outagamie.org-8)

Outagamie County is in northeast Wisconsin, covering 640 square miles along the Fox River, near the northern end of Lake Winnebago. It is the sixth-largest county by population in the state, behind Milwaukee, Dane, Waukesha, Brown, and Racine counties.
Map of the state of Wisconsin showing Outagamie County in red. Source: Wikimedia Commons, accessed March 2023.

Outagamie County is part of the Appleton Metropolitan Statistical Area, which is itself part of the Appleton-Neenah-OshkoshCombined Statistical Area. It was named for the historic Meskwaki (Fox) people.
"Outagamie", a French transliteration of the Anishinaabe term for the Meskwaki (Fox) people, means "dwellers of the other shore" or "dwellers on the other side of the stream",[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-4) referring to their historic habitation along the St. Lawrence River and south of the Great Lakes. They occupied considerable territory in Wisconsin before colonization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-5) Outagamie County was created in 1851 and organized in 1852.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-6) Before that, it was under the jurisdiction of Brown County.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has an area of 645 square miles (1,670 km 2), of which 638 square miles (1,650 km 2) is land and 7.1 square miles (18 km 2) (1.1%) is water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR1-7)

Outagamie County's government consists of an elected County Board of Supervisors, a County Executive, and 36 county agencies and departments.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-outagamie.org-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-9)
The county executive serves as its chief executive officer, participating in the legislative process with the County Board of Supervisors and exercising administrative authority and control over the county's operations, departments, offices, boards, programs, and communications.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-10)
Department heads are appointed by the county executive, subject to the approval of the board of supervisors. The county executive also appoints members to the county's boards and commissions. The county executive sets the annual budget in consultation with and subject to the approval of the board of supervisors.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-11)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-outagamie.org-8)
County Executive Tom Nelson was first elected in 2011.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-12)

**Outagamie County** ( _OW-tə-GAY-mee_)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-1) is a county in the Fox Cities region of the U.S. state of Wisconsin, in the northeast of the state. As of the 2020 census, the population was 190,705.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-2020-census-55087-2) Its county seat is Appleton.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR6-3)

Outagamie County is part of the Appleton Metropolitan Statistical Area, which is itself part of the Appleton-Neenah-OshkoshCombined Statistical Area. It was named for the historic Meskwaki (Fox) people.
"Outagamie", a French transliteration of the Anishinaabe term for the Meskwaki (Fox) people, means "dwellers of the other shore" or "dwellers on the other side of the stream",[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-4) referring to their historic habitation along the St. Lawrence River and south of the Great Lakes. They occupied considerable territory in Wisconsin before colonization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-5) Outagamie County was created in 1851 and organized in 1852.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-6) Before that, it was under the jurisdiction of Brown County.
